strengths: Significance: Sharper nonconvex stationarity guarantees for AMSGrad and corrected RMSProp would be useful. Addressing both expectation and high-probability guarantees is a worthwhile theoretical objective.

Technical approach: Section 7 combines an auxiliary momentum sequence, monotone-preconditioner telescoping, and coordinatewise gradient-history bounds into a coherent analytical framework with potential value.

Presentation and reproducibility: Explicit algorithms, assumptions, constants, and extensive proof appendices make the claims inspectable. Experiments are not inherently necessary for this theoretical contribution. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness, decisive: The AdaGrad extension is invalid. Appendices A.3 and A.6 substitute parameters into Lemma A.2, but the underlying proofs also require Lemma A.1's bound v_hat <= G_infinity^2. AdaGrad instead accumulates squared gradients, so this quantity can grow with T. Corollary 5.7 has a concrete counterexample: take the deterministic Huber loss f(x)=x^2/2 for |x|<=1 and |x|-1/2 otherwise, with x_1=10, epsilon=0.01, T=10^6, and alpha=T^(-1/2). All assumptions hold with d=L=G_infinity=1 and s=1/2. Total movement is less than 2, so every squared gradient equals 1, whereas the claimed upper bound is 0.079022. The same missing denominator control undermines Corollary 6.6.

Soundness: Even the AMSGrad proof contains incorrect intermediate bounds. Equation (A.14) uses V_hat^(-1/2) >= G_infinity^(-1) I, although Algorithm 1 includes epsilon; the available bound is (G_infinity^2+epsilon)^(-1/2) I. Equation (A.13) also assumes ||V_hat_1^(-1/2)g_1||_infinity <= 1, although this quantity can approach (1-beta_2)^(-1/2). These steps require correction before the explicit theorem constants are reliable.

Significance: The claimed strict advantage over SGD in Remarks 5.5 and 6.4 compares the proposed conditional rate with SGD's worst-case guarantee. Under the same cumulative-gradient condition along SGD's trajectory, ordinary smoothness analysis gives an average stationarity bound of Delta/(alpha T)+(L alpha d G_infinity^2/2)T^(2s-1), yielding O(sqrt(d)/T^(1-s)) after tuning. Thus the manuscript does not establish an advantage attributable to adaptivity.

Limitations and applicability: Remark 5.4 treats sparse gradients as implying s<1/2. A coordinate activated at a fixed positive frequency with nonvanishing magnitude still has cumulative norm Theta(sqrt(T)). The stronger growth assumption, its dependence on the optimization trajectory, and the prescribed stepsize's dependence on s and T need clearer discussion. No worked example establishes the relevance of the claimed favorable regime.

Originality: The potential contribution lies in refined analysis of existing algorithms, but the comparisons and references stop at 2020. For an ICML 2026 submission, the broad priority claims about high-probability guarantees and improved rates require positioning against subsequent literature.
